cited_evidence.text: AbstractCoCrNi medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) have attracted extensive attention and research because of their superior mechanical properties, such as higher ductility, strength, and toughness. This study uses molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate the cutting behavior of a gradient nanograined (GNG) CoCrNi MEA. Moreover, it explores the influence of relative tool sharpness and rake angle on the cutting process. The results show that an increase in the average grain size of the GNG samples leads to a decrease in the average resultant cutting force, as predicted by the Hall–Petch relationship. The deformation behavior shows that grain boundaries are crucial in inhibiting the propagation of strain and stress. As the average grain size of the GNG sample increases, the range of shear strain distribution and average von Mises stress decreases. Moreover, the cutting chips become thinner and longer. The subsurface damage is limited to a shallow layer at the surface. Since thermal energy is generated in the high grain boundary density, the temperature of the contact zone between the substrate and the cutting tool increases as the GNG size decreases. Molecular dynamics is applied to explore the deformation mechanism and crystal structure development of the AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys under nanoimprinting. The influences of crystal structure, alloy composition, grain size, and twin boundary distance on the mechanical properties are carefully analyzed. The imprinting load indicates that the highest loading force is in ascending order with polycrystalline, nano-twinned (NT) polycrystalline, and monocrystalline. The change in alloy composition suggests that the imprinting force increases as the Al content in the alloy increases. The reverse Hall–Petch relation found for the polycrystalline structure, while the Hall–Petch and reverse Hall–Petch relations are discovered in the NT-polycrystalline, which is due to the interactions between the dislocations and grain/twin boundaries (GBs/TBs). The deformation behavior shows that shear strain and local stress are concentrated not only around the punch but also on GBs and adjacent to GBs. The slide and twist of the GBs play a major in controlling the deformation mechanism of polycrystalline structure. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has progressed from exploring their magnetic and mechanical properties to understanding the underlying mechanisms governing their behavior. Early studies focused on the development of new high-entropy alloys with unique properties, such as high saturation magnetization and excellent strength-ductility combinations. Later research delved into the effects of composition, grain size, and twin boundary distance on mechanical properties, revealing complex relationships between these factors. The discovery of short-range ordering and its impact on dislocation-slip behavior has provided new insights into the exceptional mechanical strength of high-entropy alloys. Recent studies have also explored the use of metastable particles to enhance toughness and the application of high-entropy doping engineering to optimize electromagnetic wave absorption and dielectric properties.
decision.unsolved: Despite significant progress, the mechanistic hypothesis governing the retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys remains unclear. The relationship between composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties is complex and not fully understood, making it challenging to predict and control the behavior of these alloys. Further research is needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and develop a comprehensive understanding of high-entropy alloys.
decision.lever: investigating the effect of grain size and twin boundary distance on toughness
decision.why: Given the current understanding of high-entropy alloys, the next logical step is to investigate the effect of grain size and twin boundary distance on toughness. This can be achieved through controlled variable experiments, where the grain size and twin boundary distance are systematically varied and their impact on toughness is measured. This approach will provide valuable insights into the relationship between microstructure and mechanical properties, ultimately contributing to the development of a mechanistic hypothesis governing toughness in high-entropy alloys.
